C005.subject: Intermittent fasting
C005.object: greater long-term weight loss than caloric restriction due to improved adherence and reduced metabolic adaptation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting greater long-term weight loss than caloric restriction due to improved adherence and reduced metabolic adaptation]

[PATH:empirical] A randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting (e.g., 5:2 diet or time-restricted eating) versus continuous caloric restriction over at least 12 months, with weight loss and adherence metrics as primary outcomes. — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring long-term weight loss differences and adherence rates, addressing the claim that intermittent fasting improves adherence and reduces metabolic adaptation.

[PATH:literature] A meta-analysis of long-term (>6 months) studies on intermittent fasting versus caloric restriction, focusing on changes in resting metabolic rate (RMR) and adaptive thermogenesis. — Synthesizes existing evidence to evaluate whether intermittent fasting attenuates metabolic adaptation compared to continuous restriction, which is a key mechanism proposed in the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] A theoretical model integrating behavioral economics and metabolic physiology to predict adherence patterns and energy expenditure dynamics under intermittent versus continuous dietary regimens. — Provides a mechanistic framework to explain why intermittent fasting might lead to better adherence and less metabolic slowdown, guiding future empirical tests and refining the hypothesis.

qualifier.tension: Contrasts with the claim's focus on short-term equivalence by proposing that intermittent fasting's simpler regimen may sustain adherence and attenuate the metabolic slowdown observed with continuous caloric restriction.

C006.subject: Intermittent fasting
C006.object: caloric restriction for short-term weight loss
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting caloric restriction for short-term weight loss]

[PATH:empirical] Head-to-head RCTs comparing time-restricted feeding (e.g., 16:8) vs. continuous caloric restriction over 12-24 weeks, with weight change as primary endpoint (e.g., Lowe et al., 2020; Cienfuegos et al., 2020). — Direct randomized comparisons in the short-term domain can quantify effect size differences and assess whether intermittent fasting is inferior, equivalent, or superior to caloric restriction for weight loss.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of all RCTs (up to 6 months) comparing intermittent fasting protocols (alternate-day fasting, time-restricted feeding) to continuous caloric restriction, with subgroup analysis by adherence and calorie deficit achieved. — Synthesizing existing evidence increases statistical power to detect small differences and can reveal whether any observed inferiority is due to lower adherence or smaller energy deficit rather than physiological differences.

[PATH:empirical] Controlled feeding studies (inpatient or fully provided meals) comparing isocaloric intermittent fasting vs. continuous caloric restriction on weight loss and energy expenditure. — By controlling calorie intake precisely, these studies isolate the effect of fasting interval itself from adherence confounds, clarifying whether the fasting pattern directly impairs weight loss independent of calorie deficit.

C007.subject: Intermittent fasting with a structured behavioral maintenance program
C007.object: greater long-term weight loss maintenance beyond one year than intermittent fasting alone
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting with a structured behavioral maintenance program greater long-term weight loss maintenance beyond one year than intermittent fasting alone]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing intermittent fasting plus a structured behavioral maintenance program (e.g., cognitive-behavioral therapy, relapse prevention) versus intermittent fasting alone, with follow-up at 12, 18, and 24 months, measuring weight change, adherence, and metabolic adaptation. — Direct empirical comparison under controlled conditions would provide the strongest evidence for or against the hypothesis, addressing the tension by isolating the effect of the maintenance program on long-term outcomes.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of behavioral maintenance interventions (e.g., self-monitoring, social support, coping strategies) combined with dietary regimens for weight loss, focusing on studies with ≥12-month follow-up. — Synthesizing existing evidence across similar dietary interventions (not limited to intermittent fasting) can reveal whether structured maintenance programs generally improve long-term weight loss maintenance, supporting or challenging the specific claim.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal observational study tracking participants who self-select into intermittent fasting with or without a formal maintenance program, measuring adherence, metabolic rate, and weight trajectory over 12-24 months. — Real-world data can capture dropout and behavioral patterns that RCTs may miss, providing ecological validity and insight into whether the maintenance program mitigates common long-term failure mechanisms like metabolic adaptation or relapse.

qualifier.tension: Short-term benefits of intermittent fasting are often lost due to dropout and metabolic adaptation; adding a structured behavioral maintenance program may counteract these effects and sustain weight loss beyond one year.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intermittent fasting vs. continuous calorie restriction with follow-up ≥12 months, e.g., from Cochrane or PubMed post-2010. — Synthesizes existing long-term RCT data to assess whether intermittent fasting produces sustained weight loss beyond one year compared to standard approaches.

[PATH:empirical] Long-term prospective cohort study tracking participants in intermittent fasting programs for ≥12 months with objective weight measurements (e.g., using digital scales or clinic visits) and low attrition. — Provides direct observational evidence on real-world weight maintenance trajectories, controlling for adherence and lifestyle confounders.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of metabolic adaptation and adherence dynamics in intermittent fasting, e.g., using energy balance equations and behavioral reinforcement models. — Explores mechanistic reasons (e.g., compensatory eating, hormonal changes) that could explain why intermittent fasting may fail to sustain weight loss long-term, informing hypothesis refinement.
